rules.description: Externally-controlled input reaching a privileged chrome.* operation. The flagship privilege-escalation pattern.
Attacker-controlled data written into chrome.storage — later reads in any context become attacker-influenced.
Attacker-controlled data flowing into outbound network requests — request-forgery / SSRF surface.
Attacker-controlled data into eval / new Function / setTimeout(string) — code injection.
Attacker-controlled message echoed back through an extension message sink — most matches are noise (postMessage round-trips); the suppress list below filters the safe ones.
User-permission-gated data (bookmarks, history, cookies, identity, ...) leaving via a cross-extension or window message channel.

Fingerprint / system info (navigator.*, screen.*, chrome.system.*) leaving via a message channel. The navigator/screen carve-out lives in 'suppress' below — pure-navigator leaks are too noisy to report by default.
Data read from chrome.storage being exfiltrated through a message channel.

User-permission-gated data (cookies, history, bookmarks, identity, downloads, system info, ...) exfiltrated via an outbound network request (fetch / XHR / axios / WebSocket). The flagship data-leak pattern. Benign auth-header use is filtered by suppress-sensitive-data-request-headers below.
Untrusted server response feeding eval / new Function — classic remote code execution surface.
Server-controlled response driving a privileged chrome.* API.
Server-controlled response stored in chrome.storage for later use.
DOM / document content (innerHTML, document.URL, element values, ...) reaching a code-execution sink.
DOM / document content driving a privileged chrome.* API.
Attacker-controlled input reaching a DOM HTML-injection sink (innerHTML, jQuery .html(), React dangerouslySetInnerHTML, Vue v-html, Angular bypassSecurityTrustHtml). Classic DOM-based XSS.
DOM / document content (document.URL, element values, ...) flowing back into an HTML-injection sink — reflected DOM XSS.
Untrusted server response rendered as HTML — stored/reflected DOM XSS.
Data read from chrome.storage rendered as HTML — stored DOM XSS via a poisoned storage entry.

suppress.description: Drop every flow whose source is a native-messaging endpoint — these are out-of-process and the project intentionally treats them as opaque (matches the original isNativeOutputSource check).
Drop every flow whose sink is a native-messaging endpoint (matches the original isNativeOutputSink check).
navigator.* fingerprint sources are too noisy as DATA_LEAK; suppress that specific flow type while leaving CODE_INJECTION etc. alone.
screen.* dimensions are usually not interesting as DATA_LEAK.

Sensitive data placed in an outbound request HEADER (e.g. a cookie sent as the Cookie / Authorization header) is normal extension auth behavior, not exfiltration. Suppress only the DATA_LEAK flow type — body/URL leaks of the same data still report, and attacker-input → header (REQUEST_FORGERY) is unaffected.
window.addEventListener('message') → window.postMessage is the standard cross-frame bus and not by itself an escalation.
Page postMessage being relayed out via chrome.runtime.sendMessage to another extension is expected bridge behavior (the relay itself, not the data, is the concern).
External message coming in via onMessageExternal being echoed back is a normal request/response — not a privilege escalation by itself.
